title: The Lord turned and looked (Luke 22:54–71)
hookLine: at the third denial, Jesus turns and looks at Peter

lines: ONCE, TWICE, ABOUT AN HOUR LATER.
cards: They take Jesus to the high priest's house. Peter follows, Luke says, afar off: close enough to see, far enough to leave.

Someone has kindled a fire in the middle of the courtyard, and Peter sits down with the people around it. A servant girl looks at him a long moment: this man was with him too. Woman, I don't know him.
A little later: you're one of them. Man, I'm not. About an hour passes.
Then a third person is certain: he's a Galilean, he was with him. Matthew adds that his accent gives him away.

teach.b: Peter answers: man, I don't know what you're saying. And while he's still speaking, the rooster crows.

Then the line only Luke has, in the King James words: "And the Lord turned, and looked upon Peter. And Peter remembered the word of the Lord, how he had said unto him, Before the cock crow, thou shalt deny me thrice. And Peter went out, and wept bitterly."
Luke doesn't say exactly where Jesus is, only that he's close enough to turn and see Peter.

teach.h: TEARS ARE NOT THE END FOR PETER.
teach.b: Earlier that night, at the table, Jesus told Peter, I have prayed for you, that your faith fail not. Now, across a courtyard, one look. Luke doesn't call it angry or sad or kind.

teach.h: THE LORD TURNED, AND LOOKED UPON PETER.
teach.b: He just says the Lord turned and looked, and the look sends Peter out into the night, weeping. Preachers and painters have imagined that look ever since.
Some hear it as the opposite of a glare: the look of someone who already knew, already prayed, and still hasn't let go of him. And Peter's tears are the beginning, not the end, of his story.
Then the night goes on: the men holding Jesus mock him, blindfold him, hit him, and say, prophesy, who struck you? At daybreak the council asks him, are you the Christ?
He answers that if he told them, they wouldn't believe him. A long night, and Luke wants you to remember one moment of it: a man who just failed three times, and the face he saw when he looked up.

how: Christians read Peter's denial during Holy Week, and tradition links the rooster on some church steeples to Peter's denial and his return.

o: a member of a rebel group hiding in Jerusalem
a servant who worked in the high priest's house
someone from Galilee, the region Peter came from

s: every Gospel says Jesus turned and looked at Peter
only Luke tells of the look.
Luke tells us exactly what Jesus's face showed
Luke only says he turned and looked. the rest is left to us.

games.q: you're Peter, by the fire. a third person insists you were with him. what do you say?
o: man, I don't know what you're saying.
games.why: he denies it a third time, and while he's still speaking the rooster crows, and the Lord turns and looks at him.

practice: Bring to mind something you did that still stings; not the worst thing, just something.

Imagine someone who loves you finding out and turning to look at you: it's easy to picture a glare, so try instead a face that already knew, and isn't leaving. If you pray, you can imagine it as the face of Christ.

wordCard.voice: Galilean. What the third accuser calls Peter by his accent in the high priest's courtyard, just before the rooster crows and Peter denies Jesus a third time.

orig.note: Greek: he looked into, he fixed his gaze on. Luke's word for Jesus's look at Peter.

carryVoice: Your line: the lord looked at peter. A look that already knew, and stayed. Day five hundred eighty-two.
